newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook - all eyes on imminent Iraq bbls.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook - all eyes on imminent Iraq bbls.

text.p: A major point of uncertainty was removed from the crude oil market on Monday with the U.N. approval of Iraq's aid distributon plan, setting the stage for renewed Iraqi exports and a modest price retreat, analysts and traders said.
"I expect a response to around $19.50-19.70 a barrel, $19.00 in the worst case," said William Brown, president of W.H. Brown and Co in New York.
At 1303 EDT/1703 GMT on Monday, September light sweet crude was trading at $20.21 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), off seven cents from Friday's settlement.
The United Nations' approval of Baghdad's aid plan paves the way for the resumption of the "oil-for-food" agreement whereby Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil every six months.
"I think we'll see loading of Iraqi barrels as early as this weekend," a U.S. refiner said. "We could have Kirkuk barrels over here by the September 10."
Iraqi is expected to submit a new pricing formula for the renewed sales to the U.N. as soon as possible, probably on Tuesday, Iraqi ambassador to the U.N. Nizar Hamdoon told Reuters.
Iraq's limited return to the market is likely to push down sour crude crude prices, although competing factors such as another spate of supply disruptions in Colombia is already having an impact.
U.S. cash sour grades, for example, gained ground on Monday morning after back-to-back rebel bombings of the Cao Limn-Coveas pipeline and a damaging landslide.
West Texas Sour/Midland sold at discounts of $1.38, $1.37 and $1.35 to September West Texas Intermediate/Cushing, some seven cents stronger than Friday.
The landslide, which occurred on August 2 within 10 minutes of a rebel attack, is seen as likely to deter liftings for six to eight days.
Colombian state oil company Ecopetrol declared force majeure on crude transport along the 250,000-300,000 barrels per day (bpd) pipeline.
Operator Occidental, meanwhile, declared force majeure on the 175,000 bpd field, shutting in production.
An official declaration on export delays is seen as imminent.
On the sweet side of the market, traders noted that the market was weakening despite the narrow trans-Atlantic arbitrage.
"There's a little bit of an overhang of Nigerian barrels right now," a U.S. refiner said.
Gasoline-rich Colombian Cusiana crude traded on Friday at October WTI minus 78 cents on Friday for September 7-11 loading, off from minus 57 cents in the last September transaction, traders said.
Traders, meanwhile, continue to keep their eyes on the gasoline market for further direction.

"I think gasoline still looks tight, at least for another week. Beyond that it's hard to say," said Tom Bentz, president of High Yield Analytics in New York. "The fundamentals are a bit tighter short-term."
Indeed, analysts said gasoline is heading out of its seasonal peak, portending softer prices ahead.
"I find it difficult to believe that gasoline will continue to scream," said Brown. "I think we're going to see some falloff in implied demand in tomorrow's stats."
Brown was referring to Tuesday evening's scheduled release of oil inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API).
--Patricia Garip-Bertuol NY Energy Desk ((+1 212 859 1620))
